extracted.intended_audience: manufacturers, industrialists, entrepreneurs, business managers, and progressive farmers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical principles and evaluative standards for designing products, organizing manufacturing, and running business so as to minimize waste, serve customers, and enable high-volume low-cost production. Emphasis on product-first design, methodical testing, simplifying, and improving manufacturing methods rather than frequent product changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-first principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The big thing is the product; start with the article. Do not rush into manufacturing until you have fully satisfied yourself that utility, design, and material are the best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend time to develop confidence in the product before production (Ford spent twelve years before the Model T). Factory, organization, selling and financial plans should shape themselves to the article. Rushing into fabrication before designs are completed is a common cause of business failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize waste (materials and human effort)
rubrics_metrics.description: Waste of materials and of human effort blocks delivery of true service; eliminate useless parts and unnecessary operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study every part of an article or process to cut out entirely useless parts and simplify necessary ones. Examples: eliminate excess weight in vehicles, reduce waste motion on farms (avoid carrying water, unnecessary ladder climbs). Waste is often due to not understanding the job or carelessness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service before profit
rubrics_metrics.description: Put service before profit: profit must be the result of good service, not the basis for operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacture to serve consumer needs with high quality and low price; when service is primary, money and profit follow naturally. Avoid producing primarily for speculative gains or money-chasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of fear of the future and veneration for the past
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not fear failure or cling blindly to past practices; cautious experimentation and readiness to begin again are virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat failure as an opportunity to begin more intelligently; avoid reverence for old methods that limits progress. Maintain balanced skepticism but be willing to test promising ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disregard of destructive competition (ethical competition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A disregard of vicious competition: whoever does a thing best ought to do it; it is wrong to try to get business away from another by immoral means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compete by improving your own product and service rather than by undercutting or unfair practices that lower the condition of fellow producers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturing is transformation, not speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturing is the process of buying materials fairly and, with the smallest possible addition of cost, transforming those materials into a consumable product and giving it to the consumer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid gambling, speculating, and sharp dealing; production should be for consumption, not for making money by speculation. Keep cost-additions minimal while maintaining utility and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer improving manufacturing methods over frequent product changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Change manufacturing methods continuously; do not hastily change the product itself unless necessary for convenience or strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most cost savings come from better methods rather than new models. Ford notes few essential changes to the Model T while continuously altering operations. Use experimental prototypes to test ideas without altering mass-produced product prematurely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough testing of new ideas before altering product
rubrics_metrics.description: Test promising ideas exhaustively from every angle before deciding they are suitable for product change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain experimental models for testing; distinguish between experimental variations and official new models. Only change the product when you have confidence that the change improves utility or strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity in design (real simplicity defined)
rubrics_metrics.description: Real simplicity gives the very best service and is the most convenient in use; eliminate complexity that does not add utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design items to suit actual use; cut out useless ornamentation or unnecessary complexity. Simpler articles can be better looking, cheaper to produce, and more convenient for users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut unnecessary weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid carrying excess weight in machines or articles; extra weight is usually waste and increases cost and fuel/effort requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design structure to add strength where needed and not to add dead weight; example: avoid adding heavy chassis where added load could be carried instead. Seek materials and designs that reduce unnecessary mass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardization and interchangeability
rubrics_metrics.description: Build parts to be as nearly alike and interchangeable as possible so that no fitting is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interchangeability reduces service burden and manufacturing complexity; even with slight behavioral differences, interchangeable parts simplify repair and production. Standardization supports high-volume, low-cost production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design with substitute materials and contingency
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on a single material source; for every special material have at least one (often several) fully proved and tested substitutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work out substitutes to avoid production stoppage from material shortages or price spikes (e.g., vanadium steel example, making own glass factory when prices were driven up). Plan supply resilience into materials strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertical integration where it reduces risk/cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Make in-house parts and engines when cheaper and to avoid dependence on outside suppliers that could cripple production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance cost savings with supply security: Ford moved from making few parts to making motors and most parts to prevent being caught by market emergencies or monopolistic price increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: The chisel/cutting-edge metaphor (focus on function)
rubrics_metrics.description: An article must do what it is meant to do—the 'cutting edge' where the product touches the consumer is the crucial point of value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate products by how effectively they perform their purpose, not by peripheral attributes. A well-made product that fails to perform is useless; concentrate on the 'cutting edge' of service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design factory/organization to fit the product
rubrics_metrics.description: The factory, organization, selling, and financial plans will shape themselves to the article; start with the product and build organization around it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let product requirements determine production layout, processes, and organizational choices rather than retrofitting a product to existing organizational structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-volume, low-cost distribution strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for low-priced, high-volume production so that goods are affordable and everyone may have access; depend on volume for total profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sell at minimum profit per unit and rely on distribution volume; reduce manufacturing and distribution costs to enable low consumer prices while maintaining profits through scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximize wages/buying power within the enterprise
rubrics_metrics.description: In the process of manufacturing aim to distribute the maximum of wage—i.e., maximize buying power among those connected with the enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher wages increase buying power which supports demand for low-priced high-volume products; aligning wage distribution with low profit margins per unit supports broader prosperity and sustained demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate complexity in farming by industrial methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply industrial thinking to farming: reduce waste motion, mechanize, and arrange logically to lower costs and raise reliability/profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat farms as industrial operations—invest in pipes, machinery, logical layouts; avoid hiring extra labor as the default response to occasional extra work. Proper mechanization and planning will lower prices and raise farm profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce for consumption and quality, not ease or idleness
rubrics_metrics.description: Business exists to produce for consumption; producing for ease, idleness, or purely for money is detrimental to society and the business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the relation between value and price honest. Avoid 'public be damned' attitudes or complacency created by monopoly or speculation. Healthy business requires effort (the analog of scratching for food) to remain responsive to consumers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overcomplicating 'improvements'
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'improved' product should be genuinely better; do not change products merely for change's sake or before obtaining the best design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start making only after being satisfied that utility, design, and material are the best; if research doesn't give confidence, continue testing rather than rushing to market with a premature 'improvement.'
